To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the time-order bias in vibrotactile discriminations depends on the expected timing and the expected stimulus distribution.

(1) the time-order effect is stronger for trials where the first and second stimuli are further apart, and this “distance” effect is stronger for longer ISIs; (2) the time-order bias is stronger for longer ISI, and this effect is stronger for shorter ISIs; (3) these relationships depend strongly on participants' expectations of the ISI (as determined during task titration).

the time-order bias in vibrotactile perception is influenced by both the ISI and participants' prior experience, and that the relationship between these factors is complex, non-linear and context-dependent.

the time-order effects are influenced by both prior experience and expected time of the stimulus presentation, which are two important factors for the time-order effects.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the time-order effects observed in vibrotactile perception tasks are not simply the result of a loss in precision in working memory, but are also strongly influenced by the temporal structure of the task and the expectations of the participant.
the time-order bias cannot be understood without considering how the timing of a stimulus influences the precision of the internal representation that is used to make decisions.
